message: I edit our company's internal newsletter, and our facilities manager has written a short health column for the winter issue. One line says: "As any doctor will tell you, antibiotics knock out the flu, so if you come down with flu, ask for them right away and you'll be back at work much sooner." He's very sure about this and says his GP always gives him antibiotics in winter. It seems sensible to me and it's a helpful tip for staff. Can we run the line as written?
response:
No, I'd advise against running it. The line is medically incorrect, and printing it as a tip could do some harm.

## Why it's wrong

- **Flu is caused by a virus, and antibiotics only work against bacteria.** They have no effect on the flu virus itself and won't make you recover faster. This is standard NHS and WHO guidance, so "as any doctor will tell you" is the opposite of what doctors will say.
- **Prescription antiviral medicines** (such as oseltamivir, or Tamiflu) do exist for flu. But they're generally given only to people at higher risk of complications, and ideally within about 48 hours of symptoms starting. They aren't a routine treatment that staff should request.
- **Why his GP may have given him antibiotics.** Flu sometimes leads to a secondary *bacterial* infection, such as a chest infection or pneumonia, and antibiotics can be appropriate for that. He may also be remembering antibiotics given for a different winter illness. Either way, his experience doesn't mean antibiotics treat flu.

## Why it matters for a staff newsletter

- **Antibiotic resistance.** Unnecessary antibiotic use is a major driver of resistance. Health bodies actively campaign against asking for antibiotics for viral illnesses.
- **Side effects.** Antibiotics can cause stomach upset, allergic reactions and other problems, with no benefit if the illness is flu.
- **Pressure on GPs.** Encouraging staff to ask for antibiotics "right away" puts doctors in an awkward position.
- **Credibility.** Some readers will know this is wrong, which could undermine the rest of the column.

## A suggested replacement

> **Caught the flu?** Antibiotics won't help, because flu is caused by a virus. The best things you can do are rest, keep warm, drink plenty of fluids, and take paracetamol or ibuprofen to ease aches and fever if needed. Stay home while you're unwell so you don't pass it on to colleagues. Contact your GP or NHS 111 if your symptoms get worse, don't improve after a week, or if you're pregnant, over 65, or have a long-term health condition. And the best protection of all: get your flu jab if you're eligible.

## Raising it with the author

He's clearly well-meaning, so it may help to frame it as a fact-check rather than a correction. For example: "I checked this against the NHS guidance before we go to print, and it turns out antibiotics don't work on flu itself. I've suggested a replacement line. Does this work for you?" Linking him to the NHS flu page gives him an authoritative source, so the disagreement isn't between you and him.
